Replica.markdown: A copy of the data kept on another node, updated by applying the same changes. Replicas give read capacity, fault tolerance and locality — and a new question: how far behind may a copy be?

Primary.markdown: In single-leader replication, the one node that accepts writes, orders them in a log and ships the log to the replicas.

Replication lag.markdown: How far a replica's applied log trails the primary's. Reads from a lagging replica return older values.

Failover.markdown: Promoting a replica to primary when the primary is unreachable. Writes acknowledged by the old primary but never replicated are lost. Safe election is the subject of lesson 3.

Split brain.markdown: Two nodes both acting as primary — typically an isolated old primary still accepting writes after another was promoted. One side's writes are discarded when they meet.

Lease.markdown: Time-bounded permission to act as primary. A primary that cannot renew it (cannot reach a majority) stops serving before anyone else may be promoted.

Semi-sync.markdown: Acknowledge a write once the primary and at least one replica have it (async: the primary only; sync: every replica).

Linearizable.markdown: Every operation appears to take effect at one instant between its start and end, as if there were a single copy: once a write is acknowledged, every later read returns it or something newer.

Eventual consistency.markdown: If writes stop, all replicas eventually hold the same value. Says nothing about what reads return in the meantime.

Read-your-writes.markdown: A session guarantee: a client always sees its own completed writes.

Monotonic reads.markdown: A session guarantee: once a client has seen a version, it never later sees an older one.

Causal consistency.markdown: If a client has seen an operation, it also sees everything that operation depended on (its causal past), across clients and keys.

Quorum.markdown: The number of replicas that must answer: W for a write, R for a read, out of N. With R + W > N every read quorum overlaps every write quorum.

Sloppy quorum.markdown: When real replicas are unreachable, accept the write on other nodes (holding a hint) to stay available. Read and write quorums then may not overlap.

Hinted handoff.markdown: A node holds a write meant for an unreachable replica and delivers it when the replica returns.

Read repair.markdown: When the replies to a read disagree, the coordinator writes the newest version back to the stale replicas — before answering (blocking) or after (async). Only repairs keys that are read.

Anti-entropy.markdown: A background process that compares replicas and copies missing data, usually with Merkle trees so only differing ranges are transferred (Cassandra nodetool repair).

Merkle tree.markdown: A tree of hashes: leaves hash data ranges, parents hash their children. Two replicas compare roots and descend only where hashes differ.

Tombstone.markdown: A marker recording a delete, so the delete can replicate. Purged after gc-grace; a replica that missed the delete and is not repaired before that resurrects the data.

Last write wins.markdown: Resolve conflicting versions by keeping the one with the highest timestamp. Simple, but discards concurrent writes and trusts clocks.

Siblings.markdown: Concurrent versions of a key kept side by side because neither saw the other (detected with version vectors). The application merges them on the next write.

Network partition.markdown: Some nodes cannot exchange messages with others; messages are lost, not merely slow.

CAP theorem.markdown: During a network partition, a system cannot both stay linearizable and have every non-failing node answer every request. It says nothing about normal operation.

PACELC.markdown: If Partition: choose Availability or Consistency; Else: choose Latency or Consistency. The everyday trade-off is the "else" branch.

Partition key.markdown: The attribute that decides which partition (shard) stores a record. Queries that filter on it go to one shard; others scatter to all.

Hot partition.markdown: A partition receiving a disproportionate share of traffic — from a skewed key, a time-ordered key or one very popular item.

Consistent hashing.markdown: Nodes and keys are hashed onto a ring; a key belongs to the next node clockwise. Adding a node moves only about 1/(N+1) of the keys.

Virtual node.markdown: Each server owns many points (tokens) on the hash ring, so its share is the sum of many small arcs — much more even than one arc.

Hash slot.markdown: Redis Cluster maps every key to one of 16384 slots (CRC16 mod 16384); slots, not keys, are assigned to masters and moved explicitly.

Scatter-gather.markdown: A query the router cannot send to one shard is sent to all and the results combined: latency of the slowest shard, load on every shard.

# Primary: postgresql.conf (streaming replication)
wal_level = replica
max_wal_senders = 10

# Asynchronous by default: COMMIT returns once the WAL is flushed locally.
synchronous_commit = on
synchronous_standby_names = ''                      # async: no standby waited for

# Semi-synchronous: wait for ANY one of the listed standbys to flush the WAL.
# synchronous_standby_names = 'ANY 1 (replica_b, replica_c)'

# Synchronous to all: wait for both (a down standby stalls every commit).
# synchronous_standby_names = 'FIRST 2 (replica_b, replica_c)'

# Strongest per-commit option: the standby has also applied (visible to its readers).
# synchronous_commit = remote_apply

# Standby: postgresql.conf
# primary_conninfo = 'host=primary user=replicator'
# hot_standby = on                                  # serve read-only queries while replaying

import psycopg

primary = psycopg.connect("host=primary dbname=app")
replica = psycopg.connect("host=replica-c dbname=app")


def write(key, value):
    with primary.transaction():
        primary.execute("UPDATE kv SET v = %s WHERE k = %s", (value, key))
        lsn = primary.execute("SELECT pg_current_wal_lsn()").fetchone()[0]
    return lsn  # COMMIT has returned: acknowledged


def read(key):
    # Hot standby: may lag behind the primary (replication lag).
    return replica.execute("SELECT v FROM kv WHERE k = %s", (key,)).fetchone()[0]


def read_your_writes(key, my_lsn):
    # Session token: wait until the standby has replayed my last write, else go to the primary.
    replayed = replica.execute("SELECT pg_last_wal_replay_lsn() >= %s", (my_lsn,)).fetchone()[0]
    conn = replica if replayed else primary
    return conn.execute("SELECT v FROM kv WHERE k = %s", (key,)).fetchone()[0]

from pymongo import MongoClient, ReadPreference
from pymongo.read_concern import ReadConcern
from pymongo.write_concern import WriteConcern

client = MongoClient("mongodb://n1,n2,n3/?replicaSet=rs0")
db = client.app

# Defaults since 5.0: acknowledged by a majority of the replica set, read from the primary.
kv = db.get_collection("kv", write_concern=WriteConcern(w="majority"))


def write(key, value):
    kv.update_one({"_id": key}, {"$set": {"v": value}}, upsert=True)


def read(key):
    return kv.find_one({"_id": key})["v"]


# Fast, possibly stale: any secondary, whatever it has applied.
nearby = db.get_collection("kv", read_preference=ReadPreference.SECONDARY_PREFERRED,
                           read_concern=ReadConcern("local"))


def read_nearby(key):
    return nearby.find_one({"_id": key})["v"]


def causal(key, value):
    # A causally consistent session: reads wait until the secondary has seen my operations.
    with client.start_session(causal_consistency=True) as s:
        kv.update_one({"_id": key}, {"$set": {"v": value}}, session=s)
        return nearby.find_one({"_id": key}, session=s)["v"]

from cassandra.cluster import Cluster
from cassandra.query import SimpleStatement
from cassandra import ConsistencyLevel

session = Cluster(["n1", "n2", "n3"]).connect()
session.execute("""
    CREATE KEYSPACE IF NOT EXISTS app
    WITH replication = {'class': 'NetworkTopologyStrategy', 'dc1': 3}
""")  # N = 3 replicas of every partition
session.set_keyspace("app")

W = ConsistencyLevel.QUORUM  # wait for 2 of 3 replica acks
R = ConsistencyLevel.QUORUM  # wait for 2 of 3 replica replies (ONE = 1, ALL = 3)


def write(key, value):
    stmt = SimpleStatement("UPDATE kv SET v = %s WHERE k = %s", consistency_level=W)
    session.execute(stmt, (value, key))  # cell timestamp decides conflicts: last write wins


def read(key):
    stmt = SimpleStatement("SELECT v FROM kv WHERE k = %s", consistency_level=R)
    return session.execute(stmt, (key,)).one().v  # mismatching replicas are read-repaired


def delete(key):
    # Writes a tombstone; it is purged after gc_grace_seconds (run repair more often than that).
    session.execute(SimpleStatement("DELETE FROM kv WHERE k = %s", consistency_level=W), (key,))

import boto3

table = boto3.resource("dynamodb").Table("kv")  # partitioned by hash of the partition key "k"


def write(key, value):
    table.put_item(Item={"k": key, "v": value})


def read(key):
    # Default: eventually consistent (half the read cost; may miss a write from the last moment).
    return table.get_item(Key={"k": key})["Item"]["v"]


def read_strong(key):
    # Strongly consistent: reflects every acknowledged write; base table only, not GSIs.
    return table.get_item(Key={"k": key}, ConsistentRead=True)["Item"]["v"]


def write_if_unchanged(key, value, version):
    # Optimistic concurrency: the write fails if someone else changed the item meanwhile.
    table.put_item(Item={"k": key, "v": value, "ver": version + 1},
                   ConditionExpression="ver = :seen", ExpressionAttributeValues={":seen": version})

from redis.cluster import RedisCluster

r = RedisCluster(host="n1", port=6379)  # 16384 hash slots spread over the masters

# Slot = CRC16(key) mod 16384; the client routes each command to the slot's master.
print(r.cluster_keyslot("user:42"))

# Hash tags: only the part in {...} is hashed, so these keys share a slot (multi-key ops work).
r.set("{user:42}:profile", "...")
r.set("{user:42}:cart", "...")


def write(key, value):
    r.set(key, value)  # acknowledged by the master; replicated to its replica asynchronously


def write_and_wait(key, value):
    r.set(key, value)
    # Block until 1 replica acknowledges. Narrows, but does not close, the window for losing
    # an acknowledged write on failover: Redis Cluster is not strongly consistent.
    return r.execute_command("WAIT", 1, 100, target_nodes=r.get_node_from_key(key))

scenes.title: Replication
scenes.description: Primary–replica replication with async, semi-sync, majority and sync acknowledgements; lag, failover, split brain and multi-primary conflicts.
scenes.markdown:
### Replication: copies that follow a log

A **replica** is a copy of the data that applies the same changes in the same order. In **single-leader** (primary–replica) replication, one node — the **primary** — accepts every write, appends it to a log, and ships the log to the replicas, which replay it.

The one decision that shapes everything: **when does the primary tell the client "done"?**

| Acknowledge after… | Write latency | If the primary dies right after the ack |
|---|---|---|
| **async** — its own log only | lowest | the write may exist nowhere else → **lost** after failover |
| **semi-sync** — 1 replica has it | + one round trip | another copy exists → survives one failure |
| **majority** | + round trip to the median replica | survives any minority failure |
| **sync** — all replicas | the slowest replica's round trip | nothing lost, but **one slow or dead replica stalls every write** |

**Replication lag** is how far a replica's log trails the primary's; readers of that replica see the past.

**Failover**: a monitor notices the primary is unreachable for a timeout and **promotes** the most up-to-date replica. Writes the old primary acknowledged but never shipped are gone. If the old primary is merely cut off rather than dead, it may keep accepting writes: **split brain**. A **lease** (fencing) makes a primary that cannot reach a majority stop serving before anyone else is promoted. *How to elect safely is lesson 3.*

**The board.** *Clients* (top) shows every operation over time. *Network* lists messages in flight. Each node block holds its copy of every key: **green** = newest, **orange** = behind. Links light while messages travel and turn **red** when a partition cuts them.

**Multi-primary** (last step) lets two nodes accept writes for the same key and replicate both ways — now two writes can conflict and something must decide which survives.
scenes.prompt: You are a distributed-systems mentor preparing the learner for senior system-design interviews. Ground every claim in the live board (log positions, lag, lost writes, epochs). Ask the learner to predict before revealing. Be precise that failover here is a simplified external monitor; safe leader election is lesson 3.

scenes.title: Consistency Models
scenes.description: Read-your-writes, monotonic reads, causal and linearizable reads over lagging replicas, each checked against the real history. Each step opens with its own guarantee switched on; move Read guarantee one level down to see the anomaly it prevents.
scenes.markdown:
### Consistency models: what may a read return?

With replicas that lag, two clients can see different values at the same moment. A **consistency model** is a promise about **which values a read is allowed to return** — stated purely in terms of what clients observe, not how it is implemented.

| Model | Promise | A violation looks like |
|---|---|---|
| **Eventual** | if writes stop, replicas converge | (anything goes meanwhile) |
| **Read-your-writes** | you see your own writes | "I saved my name and the page shows the old one" |
| **Monotonic reads** | you never go back in time | a refresh shows an older score than the last one |
| **Causal** | if you saw an effect, you see its cause | a reply visible before the post it answers |
| **Linearizable** | every read sees the latest acknowledged write, as if there were one copy | C2 sees the new price, C3 *afterwards* sees the old one |

The first three are **session guarantees**: about one client's view. **Causal** covers chains between clients. **Linearizable** is about real time across everyone, and is the only one that needs coordination on every read.

**Guarantees vs. mechanisms.** Move **Read guarantee** to switch the *mechanism*: any replica · a session token (the log position of my last write) · a version token per key · a causal token (the highest position I have seen) · always read the primary. A replica holding a token waits until it has caught up — the latency each guarantee costs shows in *p99*.

**Reading the tokens.** Every value on a node shows the log position that wrote it: `post = 1 @1` was the primary's 1st log entry, and `@0` is the initial value. A client's status line shows the token it carries (`token log ≥ @2`, or per key `s ≥ @1`); its read message says `needs @2`, and while the chosen replica is behind the client shows `waits: N3 has @1, needs @2`.

**The checker.** Nothing on the board trusts the mechanism. A history checker labels every read with the **weakest guarantee it breaks**, and searches for a single order of all operations that respects real time (linearizability). The **guarantee matrix** (right) runs every scenario under every mechanism.

> *Isolation* (lesson 1) orders **transactions**; *consistency models* order **operations on copies**. A system can have one without the other; *strict serializability* is both.
scenes.prompt: You are a distributed-systems mentor. Define each consistency model by what clients observe, then the mechanism that provides it. Use the history checker labels and the guarantee matrix as ground truth. Keep isolation (transactions) and consistency (replicas) distinct.

guides.text: C1 saves profile v=2, then reloads; each reload lands on a different replica. **Read-your-writes**: C1 carries the log position of its write, and a replica that is behind **waits** before answering. **Predict** how long the slow reload waits, then play. Switch Read guarantee to *eventual* to see the reload that shows v=1.

C2 refreshes repeatedly while the lagging N3 is one of its replicas. **Monotonic reads**: C2 remembers the newest version of s it has seen (s ≥ @n), so N3 waits rather than send it back in time. Switch to *eventual* to see the score go back; *read-your-writes* does not help, because C2 wrote nothing.

C3 reads C2's reply, then opens the post it answers. **Causal**: C3 carries the highest log position it has seen (log ≥ @2, the reply), so N3 waits until it has everything up to the reply, including the post. Switch to *monotonic reads*: they are per key, so the reply is visible and the post is not.

C1's price change is acknowledged; then C2 and C3 read the price. **Linearizable**: every read goes to the primary, so once the write is acknowledged everyone sees it, at the cost of a trip to N1. Switch to *causal*: C3, reading nearby after C2, sees the old price, though no session guarantee is broken.
Each cell ran one scenario under one mechanism. ✗ names the weakest guarantee that broke; ✓ shows the p99 latency paid. Which is the cheapest mechanism for each product feature?

steps.title: Monotonic reads
steps.description: C2 refreshes repeatedly while the lagging N3 is one of its replicas. **Monotonic reads**: C2 remembers the newest version of s it has seen (s ≥ @n), so N3 waits rather than send it back in time. Switch to *eventual* to see the score go back; *read-your-writes* does not help, because C2 wrote nothing.
steps.prompt: The read guarantee is monotonic reads (a version token per key). Show C2's token growing as it reads, and N3 holding a read until it catches up. Then have the learner try eventual (s goes from 1 back to 0) and read-your-writes (still broken: C2 has no writes), and explain the difference between the two session guarantees.

steps.title: Causal consistency
steps.description: C3 reads C2's reply, then opens the post it answers. **Causal**: C3 carries the highest log position it has seen (log ≥ @2, the reply), so N3 waits until it has everything up to the reply, including the post. Switch to *monotonic reads*: they are per key, so the reply is visible and the post is not.
steps.prompt: The read guarantee is causal (a causal token). Show that the reply is entry @2 and the post @1, and that N3 waits until it has applied @2. Then have the learner switch to monotonic reads and explain why a per-key token cannot catch this: the post and the reply are different keys. Mention MongoDB causally consistent sessions (afterClusterTime).

steps.title: Linearizability
steps.description: C1's price change is acknowledged; then C2 and C3 read the price. **Linearizable**: every read goes to the primary, so once the write is acknowledged everyone sees it, at the cost of a trip to N1. Switch to *causal*: C3, reading nearby after C2, sees the old price, though no session guarantee is broken.
steps.prompt: The read guarantee is linearizable (read the primary). Show every read crossing to N1 and the latency it costs. Then have the learner switch to causal and explain why that history satisfies causal consistency yet is not linearizable: C2 and C3 never interacted, so no causal chain forces C3 to see the write, but in real time the write had finished.

steps.title: Read the guarantee matrix
steps.description: Each cell ran one scenario under one mechanism. ✗ names the weakest guarantee that broke; ✓ shows the p99 latency paid. Which is the cheapest mechanism for each product feature?
steps.prompt: Drill: for a profile page, a news feed, a comment thread and a stock price, have the learner pick the weakest guarantee that is still correct, justify it from the matrix, and name the latency cost.

scenes.title: Quorum Reads and Writes
scenes.description: N, R and W in a leaderless store: overlap, availability, latency, and four ways R + W > N still is not linearizable.
scenes.markdown:
### Quorums: tune consistency per request

**Leaderless** replication (Dynamo, Cassandra, Riak): any node can **coordinate** a request. Each key has **N** replicas. A write succeeds once **W** replicas acknowledge; a read asks **R** replicas and returns the newest version among their replies.

If **R + W > N**, every read quorum overlaps every write quorum in at least one replica — so a read *should* meet the latest write. Fewer nodes to wait for means lower latency and higher availability: R = W = 1 is fast and survives N − 1 failures, but reads can be stale.

**Try it:** set N, R, W and kill replicas. A request that cannot reach enough replicas is **rejected** immediately; one whose replies are too slow **times out**. The **quorum matrix** (right) runs the selected scenario for every R × W at this N.

**Why R + W > N is not enough for linearizability** — four runnable counterexamples:

1. **A read during a slow write.** The write has reached 1 of 3 replicas. Reader A's quorum includes it (new value); reader B, *after A finished*, picks two replicas without it (old value). Fixed by **blocking read repair**: A writes the newest value back before answering.
2. **A failed write stays.** The client is told the write failed (too few acks before the timeout), but one replica stored it. Later readers disagree about whether it happened — nothing rolls it back.
3. **Sloppy quorum.** When the real replicas are unreachable, fallback nodes accept the write (holding a *hint*). The write and read quorums no longer overlap.
4. **Last write wins with clock skew.** Conflicts are settled by timestamp; a node with a fast clock makes an *earlier* write win, silently discarding a later acknowledged one.

> Cassandra: consistency level per statement (ONE / QUORUM / ALL / LOCAL_QUORUM); linearizable compare-and-set needs lightweight transactions (Paxos, lesson 3). DynamoDB does not expose N, R, W at all — only eventually or strongly consistent reads.
scenes.prompt: You are a distributed-systems mentor. Use the live board and the computed quorum matrix. Be precise: R + W > N gives overlapping quorums, not linearizability; explain each counterexample from the actual messages and replies. Relate settings to Cassandra consistency levels without overstating the model.

steps.title: Fast but stale
steps.description: **R = W = 1**: one ack, one reply. Latency drops — and C2 reads from N3 before the write reaches it. **Predict** which reads are stale, then play.
steps.prompt: Ask the learner to predict which of C2's reads are stale with R = W = 1. Then relate the result to R + W ≤ N and to Cassandra consistency level ONE.

steps.title: Failures and availability
steps.description: One replica down: W = 2 still succeeds. Raise **Replicas down** to 2 — now every request is rejected. Try W = 1 with R = 3, and R = 1 with W = 3.
steps.prompt: Explain the availability side of the trade-off: a request needs W (or R) live replicas. Have the learner find settings that keep writes available with two replicas down, and say what they give up.

steps.title: The quorum matrix
steps.description: Every R × W cell ran this scenario. Change **N** and **Replicas down** and watch the safe (R + W > N) corner, the stale corner and the unavailable edge move.
steps.prompt: Walk through the computed matrix: cells with R + W ≤ N read stale, cells needing more live replicas than exist fail, and the latency cost grows with R and W. Ask the learner to pick R and W for a read-heavy, a write-heavy and a must-not-lose workload.

steps.title: Counterexample 1 · read during a write
steps.description: R + W > N, yet reader A sees x=1 and reader B, **after A finished**, sees x=0. Switch **Read repair** to *blocking*.
steps.prompt: Explain why this history is not linearizable even though every quorum overlaps: the write is still in flight, A's quorum includes the one replica that has it and B's does not. Blocking read repair makes A copy the newest value to a second replica before answering, so B's quorum must meet it.

steps.title: Counterexamples 2 and 3
steps.description: C1 is told its write **failed**, yet C2 reads it — and then C3 does not. Switch Scenario to **Sloppy quorum**: fallbacks N4, N5 accept the write and C2 cannot see it.
steps.prompt: Explain both: a failed write is not rolled back (the client must treat a timeout as unknown, not as "did not happen"), and a sloppy quorum trades the overlap guarantee for availability during a partition, repaired later by hinted handoff.

steps.title: Counterexample 4 · clock skew
steps.description: N1's clock runs 6 ticks fast. C2's write of x=2 comes **after** C1's x=1 was acknowledged, but carries an older timestamp — so x=1 wins everywhere.
steps.prompt: Explain last-write-wins: replicas keep the version with the highest timestamp, which needs synchronized clocks. A skewed clock silently discards a later acknowledged write. Mention that Cassandra uses client or coordinator timestamps; the alternative is to keep siblings (next scenes) or use consensus (lesson 3).
